title: PM changes tack on need for digital safety laws
full_text:
Anthony Albanese has cited the rise of misinformation and disinformation to justify Labor’s proposed digital safety regime, departing from his government’s previous insistence that the laws are strictly aimed at bolstering online protections and user empowerment.
Speaking on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, the Prime Minister also described Labor’s proposed digital duty of care as a “very positive move” in response to political polarisation.
The duty, which Labor unveiled draft legislation for earlier this month, would place an onus on social media platforms and other online services to shield users from “seriously harmful material and conduct”.
While the draft legislation explicitly defines such content, it also includes a provision that would enable the communications minister to designate additional harms, prompting warnings from legal experts, civil liberties advocates, the Human Rights Commission and the Coalition, who all caution it could be used to regulate speech.
The Trump administration echoed those concerns on Tuesday, with the US embassy in Canberra warning that the proposed duty would amount to “facilitating censorship”. “A framework that empowers governments to enforce vague definitions of “harm” risks becoming a mechanism for viewpoint-based censorship, as platforms will be incentivised to over-moderate speech that should be protected to avoid regulatory penalties,” the embassy said.
Speaking at an event hosted by the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of AI, hosted at the UN headquarters in New York, Mr Albanese pushed back against the criticism, insisting the measures were the “opposite” of government control. “It’s about giving everyone control over their own lives,” he said.
But he then proceeded to tie the reforms to “misinformation, disinformation and increased polarisation”, saying digital services were “having an impact on our entire society and how it functions”. “People are moving away from the centre and more and more to the extremes, be they of the left or the right, and that is why we think that this is a very positive move that we are [putting] forward,” he said.
The comments contrast with those by Communications Minister Anika Wells, who insisted the duty “isn’t about misinformation” just a fortnight ago.
“This is about basic safety standards that Australians should expect from an industry that is selling them and their children products,” Ms Wells told News24 on September 9.
Since unveiling the reforms, Labor has strenuously rejected claims that the power to designate new forms of harm creates a pathway to censorship. It has also repeatedly sought to distance the proposed changes from its abandoned misinformation and disinformation bill.
After the Coalition vowed to vote against the mooted duty, opposition communications spokeswoman Sarah Henderson said the remarks raised an “obvious question” about who would determine what constituted “harmful” misinformation, disinformation and other political content.
“Under Labor’s own exposure draft, Anika Wells has that power. That is exactly why strong safeguards for lawful speech, journalism and political debate matter,” she said in a statement.
The Greens have also questioned the authority granted to the communications minister, with the minor party’s digital rights spokesman David Shoebridge last week declaring: “I don’t think you should have unlimited ministerial discretion”.
Echoing those concerns, the Digital Industry Group Inc, an industry body representing major tech platforms including Google, Microsoft and Meta, challenged what it viewed to be excessive discretion by the communications minister to determine what constituted harm.
“This raises concerns about the duty being overly restrictive and burdening the implied freedom of political communication where there are no public interest exceptions,” DIGI said in response to the exposure draft.
